And again, you told the police, with regard to the same circumstance, you said the following: "Immediately after the killing of the family of my son Naser, a camouflaged attacker with a bottle in his hand was pouring a liquid all over the room."

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it started a fire in two places and then left the house?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, no. I said quite clearly, as he got into the house, on the left-hand side, he threw gasoline, he set it on fire, and on the right-hand side he set fire to a chair that was next to the late Sejo's bed. And while he was doing this, this other one had finished whatever else he had set out to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, where was this chair, on what side in relation to the entrance door?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the right-hand side. On the right-hand side as you enter the room. That is where the little bed was, and the chair between the bed and the door. That's where the chair was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the U.N. papers relating to the statement you made to (redacted) you said something different. You told (redacted) the following: "They poured petrol, which they carried in glass bottles, all over the rooms, including the couch behind which the witness was hiding." And then the house was set on fire. So there you say that both of them were torching the house, that is to say, pouring gasoline all over the house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Moskowitz?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: It's probably now a little late, but I didn't want to interpose. I have an objection to referring to this statement from (redacted) to Payam Akhavan. This is clearly not a statement that the witness is familiar with, or signed or read, and it seems a bit unfair to task him with a statement that was given third-hand to somebody else. It's not, in my view, a fair cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. Also, because I understand that (redacted)is being called by you as a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Just one remark if I may. Mr. Akhavan was heard, and he said he made this statement according to the notes that were given to him by (redacted), and that he relied, while composing this statement, on the notes that he had. So these are not people who happened to be there and who happened to hear something, but these are people who were qualified in terms of following certain events. I think that what the official report says is a fact that bears certain weight and a certain force, but I won't go further into that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a few more things in relation to these statements, because several statements were made, and we think that all of them carry a weight of their own, so we want to say a few more things about them. In the statement made before this court, you said that, first of all, Zoran walked into the room?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Immediately after him Mirjan?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you repeated that on several occasions, so there's no confusion with regard to that. However, in the statement you gave to the investigator, on the 13th of October, 1994, and the 14th of October, 1994, you gave a completely different description of events and I'm going to read that to you now. You said the following: "When I looked towards Naser I saw Zoran Kupreskic enter the room, and he was bending forward and holding a gun with both hands as if he was getting ready to shoot. I recognised Zoran, although he had colour or bands on his face. As Zoran walked into the room, he turned to the right where Naser stood. Naser was wearing his underwear, so he was not armed at all. When Zoran saw Naser, he immediately fired a burst of gunfire which killed Naser. Zoran then turned towards Zehrudina who was still lying only the mattress, shot a burst of gunfire into her, but did not kill her with it. Then he started walking towards the couch on which Elvis was. As he started, I saw Mirjan Kupreskic enter the living-room." Now, that is to say after two killings -- now, please just listen to this to the end. "Although he also had paint or some kind of band on his face, I did recognise Mirjan because I've known him ever since he was born. Mirjan was carrying bottle of something which looked like gasoline. He went to the couch which was on the eastern side of the living-room and poured some gasoline on it. Then he went to the armchair that was right to the entrance, on the right-hand side to the entrance to the living-room. He poured out this gasoline, and then he lit a match and set the armchair on fire. That was all that I saw, because I fell on my stomach by the couch where Elvis was. I'm quite sure that someone, and I'm sure that it was Zoran, because I did not see whether Mirjan had any arms or not, came to the couch and fired three bursts of gunfire on me." In this statement you said that Mirjan walked into the room after the first attacker, who, according to you, was Zoran, killed your daughter-in-law and son.

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: At the same time, when Zoran walked in, immediately --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic. Mr. Ahmic. You said this at the trial.

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you how come you told the investigator, whom you had talk to for two days, describe the event in the following way: That Mirjan walked in after two killings were already committed, and then when he started moving towards the couch where your grandson was --

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- Mirjan managed to start a fire in two places in the room and only then does the firing take place which you cannot even see.

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, this is a moment in all these events. These are a few seconds. Please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe you. That is correct. That is correct. However, I'm just trying to tell you something. You are claiming today, with 100 per cent certainty, and you said that when you were testifying on Friday, that the events happened in the way in which you have explained them.

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I am showing you that you described these events in a different way before. So you cannot be that certain now.

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm 100 per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are 100 per cent sure?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And these mistakes were, I presume, made by others, is that what you think?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Perhaps they were my mistakes, but I think that this is true and truthful. When Zoran got in, then Mirjan followed, and he poured gasoline, he set it on fire, and then poured gasoline on the chair on the right-hand side and set it on fire. While this was being done, the other one committed the killings, that is of the late Naser and my late daughter-in-law, and the late Elvis. And at that point I was already lying on the floor. And I said a few minutes ago this is something that took place within a few seconds practically. It's not that someone came there to take pictures or to make a film.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But in those -- you have several versions, four versions about these few seconds. Perhaps you cannot remember certain things, but every time you give different answers. So just a bit more now in relation to the rifle that was already mentioned. You said, at the trial and then today again, that you cannot exactly recall the rifle that Zoran Kupreskic had?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I'm not sure. I'm not 100 per cent sure, because I was not focusing on the weapon. I was looking at the person who was doing this terrible thing, killing all my nearest and dearest and trying to kill me too at the same time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 13th of October, in the statement made to the investigative judge, you said the following: "The rifle that he carried was about 48 centimetres long. At the top it had a round drum." On the 13th of October, 1994, you were shown an automatic rifle, a MGV automatic rifle, and it seems to me that that is precisely the kind of gun that Zoran had on the 16th of April, 1993. So you explain in detail the rifle. You say how big it is, you say where the drum is. You say that that is the kind of rifle it was, that it seems to you that that was the rifle. So these are very precise descriptions.

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. They showed me this rifle, but it is true that it was shown to me at that moment, that rifle. Perhaps it was a different rifle, a bigger one, I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So why did you say then that it seemed to you that that was the rifle in question?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: How can I say? Perhaps it was even bigger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But these are your statements, you know, that's why I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I told you very nicely that everyone should try to put himself into that kind of situation, and I'd ask anyone how they would feel in that kind of circumstance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I can imagine that. Tell me, how long did this event in the house -- how long did it go on for?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: A few seconds. Just like this. As long as it takes to clap your hands. That's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Just one more thing that I wish to ask you; who was it that was actually shooting in the house? Because there are differences between your different statements with regard to that particular matter too. In the Court you said it was Zoran Kupreskic who shot.

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That he killed Naser, Zehrudina, Elvis and the baby, because Mirjan didn't have a rifle?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know if he had a rifle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you didn't see him with a rifle?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know whether he had a rifle or not, because Mirjan was bending forward. He was squatting, so I'm not sure. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I mean, how did he walk into the room?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: He walked in behind Zoran. He was bending forward, I'm telling you, and then he crouched and then he started shooting at the bed. So he was --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he was practically crouching?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Zoran?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Zoran was standing straight up, but his head was bent forward a bit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How could you see Mirjan if he was crouching and if he came after Zoran?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: How could I not see him? How do I see you now?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you have a table there. You do have a table there in the room.

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I know, it's a table but it didn't bother me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It didn't bother you?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, it didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And now in relation to this fact, you told the police the following: "Immediately upon entering the house," that is the 22nd of April, "One of them fired from the hallway, there was a burst of gunfire from the hallway, while the other one saw the light in the room and my son Naser standing up, and he burst fire -- he opened fire, and going into the room killed my daughter-in-law Zehrudina, and the little boy Elvis, who was still asleep in the bed with her. As they shot at them, everything was quiet for a moment and then my grandson began crying again."

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "And the killer returned."

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Did he not return, he just turned round and opened fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I'm reading from this document here. "And fired a burst of gunfire into the child's cot." From this statement it would appear that both were firing, one on the verandah and one on the other --

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. No, this burst of gunfire that was mentioned refers to the killing of the late Naser and not on the verandah, not shooting on the verandah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. The statement given to the investigative judge, in it you say that they came into the room, one of them opened fire on Naser, and you fell behind the couch where your grandson was sleeping, and you heard -- "I heard and felt them shooting at my daughter-in-law and son." That is, once again, in the plural, so you're referring to individuals opening fire, in the plural.

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. It was only one individual who shot -- opened fire in the room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now to wind up, let me show you that in the transcript of the tape that we listened to, you also used the plural, and you stated the following: "In the meantime, the HOS members -- not the HOS, the HVO army came to the door, they burst open the door with their foot and opened fire on the verandah. They entered the room, the light was on --

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, the light was on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- and as they saw my son standing, they fired at him immediately, and I open the door slightly ajar and period through. They then opened fire on my daughter-in-law, and my second grandson, my son, and they went to the door. However, the little boy started crying in the cradle." And from that we can deduce that two men opened fire?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, only one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Only one you say?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me, you say in your statement that you made sure what had happened to Naser, you saw him. When Naser fell down, when the house was set on fire, you went to see -- you went to look at Naser. You said that there was blood?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I glanced at him and in front of his chest there was a pool of blood. I saw it with my own eyes. And I opened the window and tried to jump out to escape to try to save my life, but when I looked through the window I saw, in Vlatko's yard, two or three Croatian soldiers. Vlatko came up to the house --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, we won't go further into that. You told us about that and that is not the part that we are contesting. Tell me, please, did you look to see what happened to Elvis and Sejad? Did you see them or not?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: How do you mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go up to them to see what happened?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. I didn't go up to any of the people, because I -- it was enough for me to look at them to see what had happened, because it all took place in the 68 square metres of my home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you didn't go up to any of them afterwards?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the transcript of the videotape, you state that you tried to pull the children out into the room.

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: This is what went through my head. I thought how I -- I wondered how I could save them, but that was all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said, "I tried to pull the children out into the room over there where I was, so as to localise this in some way, so that the children would not burn if they were -- as they had been killed to prevent them from being burnt."

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, that is something I thought of doing, but I didn't, in fact, pull them out of the room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, tell me just where Elvis was sleeping, what place, what position Elvis -- yes.

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Elvis was asleep on the couch.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is the same couch behind which you say you hid?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, we read out a moment ago from a police statement, where you say that, "The soldiers, upon entering the room, killed my daughter-in-law Zehrudina and the little boy Elvis, who was still sleeping in the bed with her."

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Not with her in the bed, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But these are all statements that you signed. That is why I'm asking you once again, why does this not correspond to what you're saying now?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Then it was the mistake -- a mistake made by the individual who wrote that, because Elvis had his own couch for sleeping on. The late Sejo had his little cot for sleeping in, and the late Naser and his wife Zehrudina had a mattress on the floor and that is where they slept.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you make these explanations earlier on?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. I always explained that in the way that, in fact, it was. I can't explain it in any other way than the way it happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us now go -- move forward. You said that below the house there was a basement. The basement was equipped for living in. Was it a room with a kitchen or what did it look like?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, it was a room with a kitchen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. A room with a kitchen. Did you have a toilet there?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: What did you say?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a toilet?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, no. I didn't understand you. No, there was no toilet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So anybody living in the basement would have to use the field toilet?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, in an outhouse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you sometimes spend some time in the basement?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, we all did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the summer months?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: In the summer season, and in winter too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you often slept down in the basement?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, we did. If I couldn't find peace upstairs, I would go down for a bit of peace and sleep downstairs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you sleep there at night?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, at night too, or when I wanted a rest during the day, both ways.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that means that in the -- on the premises below -- down in the basement, you needed -- you had everything you needed?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. We had running water as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, whether you had a dog?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, we had a dog.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was an Alsatian?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A German sheep dog?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, no, it was a vagabond, and we would give the dog food and it sort of stopped with us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A stray dog. Did it go into the house?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, it never entered the house. And dogs will never enter the house because dogs are made to live outside. But we all gave it food. We all fed it. I fed him too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was he with you when the events took place?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: In the house you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, in front of the house. Did you see the dog?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I didn't, but I heard the barking of a dog, and then there was a burst of gunfire and then nothing more was heard from the dog, and I thought that the dog had been killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the dog tied?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, it wasn't tied. It moved around freely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, of the Croatian houses, which house was the first house down the road from your house?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Down the road? Yes. Well, I don't know. My house lies between two roads, the road towards Ahmici and the road leading towards Pirici, so I am there in the corner, between the two roads.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that is going downwards?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I am linked to the road going towards Ahmici on the main road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And whose house is the first house on that road?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is the house of Vlatko Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You said that this event took place very quickly, it lasted two or three seconds.

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, it was very quick, over very quickly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me whether Naser worked in the footwear shop between Vitez and Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, he was employed there all the time until his very last -- until the last day, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, did he go with friends for a drink after work and to relax with his friends after work?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, this depended on how much free time he had. It depended on whether he had any money or not. But at that time, we had very little money. We had to work a great deal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But did he do that on occasion? Did he have friends with whom he would go out for a drink after work?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, of course he had friends, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just a bit more -- to go back to the events in the house. You said that the door opened, that is, that the hinges were on the right-hand side of the door.

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you were standing in the doorway or in front of the door. Which?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, along the -- the line of the wall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the point when you saw the attacker moving towards you, at that particular moment, or when he was moving towards Elvis, rather, you said you fell down and you were unconscious.

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I fell into a coma at that point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, how did you fall?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I fell with my head up against the wall. How that happened, I can't explain it myself. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But, according to the picture that the Prosecutor showed us, you fell with your legs towards the north and you were lying straight and you were lying on your stomach and you hit your head against the wall. How did you do that?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I didn't perform it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I'm asking you. You fell on your stomach.

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now -- where did you hit your head?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not the wall?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Not the wall, no. I hit it on the floor. That is what I think. Perhaps I did hit my head against the wall as well, but I found myself prostrate on the floor against the couch and the wall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the manner in which you fell was that, standing up straight by the door, you fell on your stomach and along the wall, vertically along the wall?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I can't explain that moment to you, how it happened. Perhaps I made a step towards Naser. Then at that moment, I had a heart attack and fell down and my brain reacted in that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you watching Naser at that time, at that moment? Were you looking towards him, because you said that you went towards Naser.

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I said perhaps I made a step towards Naser, and they were all before my eyes as I was standing there in that second.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have three more questions, but I would like a closed session, please, for those three questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. (Closed session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: (Open session) Cross-examined by Mr. Krajina:

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: With your permission, I wish to ask the witness whether he said that Vlatko Kupreskic was stealing the things that belonged to his son.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Could you please answer this question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's me you're asking? I did not say anywhere that Vlatko Kupreskic was stealing things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Just a minute --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Nothing else that we're interested in. Thank you. That will do. And now, with the permission of the Court, I wish to address Sakib Ahmic, the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, I am addressing you only to clarify a certain point from your statement, nothing else. Namely, at the trial on the 4th of September this year, that is to say, just before the break, the last day of the trial before the break, you said that on the morning of April 16th, 1993, as you were watching through the window of your room, you saw, in the yard of Vlatko Kupreskic, you saw a soldier of the HVO and that therefore you did not dare go out of the house and jump through the window; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you now say whether you recognise that soldier?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I didn't recognise him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. President, in the transcript from the trial on the 4th, on page 43, line 16, it has been said mistakenly that this soldier was Vlatko Kupreskic. So could this mistake please be rectified? I don't know how it happened, but it is there and it is in the transcript, and we found it on our laptops. And so let me just finish this --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm afraid that a mistake was made there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Krajina, sorry, are you saying that the witness mistakenly mentioned Vlatko Kupreskic, the soldier being Vlatko Kupreskic? So was this mistake --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Sorry. Are you claiming that he did not say Vlatko Kupreskic was the soldier, did not identify the soldier with Mr. Kupreskic? So the name --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: That is what he said now too. But probably it is the word "yard" that was missing, Vlatko Kupreskic's yard.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can we please understand each other correctly? Please. As I was standing at the window waiting for a good moment to jump out, I saw two or three soldiers in Vlatko's yard down there. I didn't dare jump out. I was afraid that they would catch me alive because when I saw that they had killed all of my people and that I had survived, in all this killing, I was afraid that they would catch me alive and that they would torture me and finally kill me and that no one would ever hear of me --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We know that. We heard all of that.

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: At that moment, Vlatko --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm sorry, that's not what I asked. But in your statement you said somewhat later, as you were watching through the window, you were wondering whether to jump out or not and you saw one soldier, a soldier.

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we are just talking about that one soldier, and you said that you did not recognise him, and in the transcript we saw a mistake. It was mistakenly written down in the transcript. So we have finished this. Thank you. Now, just one more question, Mr. President. Just one more. Mr. Ahmic, can you tell me what do you mean when you say soldier, "bojovnik"? Are you referring to an armed person in uniform?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: For me, that is precisely what soldiers are, that is, young men under arms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Uniformed and armed?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Susak, Counsel Susak?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. President, as usual, I have only one brief question, perhaps two for the witness. Cross-examined by Mr. Susak:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that, I think, in Barin Gaj there was some shooting and that five or six Bosniaks were killed there; is that correct? Is that the right place, the right location? Or was it somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm sorry, I did not say ever that anyone was killed in Barin Gaj, but there is one thing that I did say: On the 17th of April of 1993, I was withdrawing in Barin Gaj. As I was getting out of Barin Gaj, I encountered five or six young men who were entering Barin Gaj with rifles and they were moving towards Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I wanted to ask you something else: Did you know Nenad Dzidic?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Nenad Dzidic?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Did you hear of him, what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Ah, Nenad, yes. Yes, I remember him now. Nenad and Muharem; they were two brothers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I heard that they were both killed. I heard that they were both killed in the area of Zume.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I wanted to ask you -- well, all right -- whether you know whether it happened in that particular place or elsewhere as you were moving in that direction, as you were withdrawing towards your mother's house?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, no, no. It was completely in the opposite direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand there are no further questions from Defence counsel, so we can now take a break, a 30-minute break. I imagine the Prosecutor would like to re-examine the witness. Is it so, Mr. Moskowitz?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. So a 30-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to ask that these statements be tendered into evidence, and may I hand them to the registrar? I can enumerate them if you wish. It is the statement of the 13th of October and 14th of October, 1994. The minutes from the 1st of October, 1993; the statement made on the 22nd of April, 1993; and the statement given to the investigators dated the 12th of November, '97; as well as the statement from the 2nd of September, 1995. Those are the documents, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I would just say, Your Honour, that for completeness sake, we would offer as well the statement on February 20th, 1994, which should complete the set.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, all the statements made by the witness. Yes. All right. Admitted into evidence. Good. Mr. Moskowitz?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Re-examined by Mr. Moskowitz.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon Mr. Ahmic. Just several questions for you before you're through. You were asked questions about Vlatko Kupreskic, and just to make it absolutely clear, did you see Vlatko Kupreskic on April 16, 1993?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were you when you saw Vlatko Kupreskic that day?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was precisely at the window of my room, from which position I saw Vlatko Kupreskic, who was moving from the house and the yard of Suhrija, my Suhrija, and he went past his own house and behind the house, and went behind the house and I couldn't see him any more, because he went round by the back side and under the house. And while he was moving in this direction, I think that he had something under his left arm, that he was carrying something. What it was, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall how he was dressed?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. He had a blue coat on, and under the coat what he had, I don't know. It was a blue worker's overall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you were also asked about -- about your mother. Could you tell us, in what year your mother was born?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: My mother was born -- she is 1909, born in 1909. She is 90 years old.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does she live with you now?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, she does. My mother is with me. And she is in a poor state of health because the years have taken their toll. She cannot move much. She needs care and attention, and she needs medical attention and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And does she sometimes get things confused in her mind?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, it's normal that it is somebody who -- she's an old woman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Of course, we are all aware this was a leading question. On the other hand, I think it's not -- I mean, it is relevant but it's not a crucial matter. We were all aware that it was a leading question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, we respect the age of his mother and we're not going to call his mother as a witness, and it's normally -- it's quite normal that she should lose herself here and there, so there's no point in suggesting what happened nine years ago and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Moskowitz?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I don't want to belabour this either, but let me just ask one more follow-up question to that just to finish this area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall a time when I visited you and your mother in Zenica, and could you tell us what your mother -- who your mother thought I was?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you mother think I was?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I remember very well. When the gentleman, Mr. Albert came, she thought he was the doctor. She thought he was the doctor who had come to examine her, and she expected an examination. She thought he would take her blood pressure. She expected some prescriptions, him to write some prescriptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, you know that we are prohibited to asking questions as to what a third party thought, and now the witness is precisely saying what his mother thought when the Prosecutor turned up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Why? I think it's quite appropriate, because the Prosecutor is asking about the -- asking the witness about his work. Yes, you are right. On reflection, you're right. Mr. Moskowitz, move on. You're right, because he's asking the witness to report about his mother's attitude vis-à-vis the Prosecutor hearsay but --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Only offered to show the state of mind of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes but probably you can simply move on, because it's not, as I say, a crucial matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were also asked about a light in the room that was hanging over the table. Could you describe how far from the ceiling this light was hanging?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, the light was about 20 centimetres from the ceiling. About 20 centimetres from the ceiling. But it was the light of this room, of the living-room, and it doesn't stop us from moving around or anything. It's not in the way in any way. It had its height, just as in all the other rooms and all the other things in the room. It caused no -- it didn't hamper anything. It didn't get in the way of me, or the women, or the children or the guests coming to the house. It wasn't in the way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And while you were standing in your door, the doorway of your bedroom, looking towards the entrance doorway into that room, could you describe whether or not this light hanging over the table was in your line of sight in any way or obstructed your view in any way?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. In no way did it obstruct my view.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were also asked about the table, and I'll ask you the same question about the table. Did the table obstruct your view in any way of the entrance door to the room?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. Not at all. The table was no obstruction, nor could it have been, nor did it form any obstruction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Defence counsel also asked you about a disciplinary action that was filed against you while you were employed. Could you tell us how many years were you employed?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: For a full 40 years, and that -- those are my full years of service, and I retired after them. I worked for all of 40 years. I never used any social funds. I thought that I would get a flat when I retired. I requested a flat, 14, 15 years, but I never got what was due to me following my 40-year investment into the housing fund. I paid money into the housing fund, and I was not able to buy a one-room flat, but I think that I could have bought a four or five-room flat, according to the investments I had made over the 40 years of service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just to be clear, this 40 years of employment covered more than one employment or one job; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, more than one job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in 40 years of employment, you had one reprimand over a vacation dispute. Is that the bottom line? Is that what you remember?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could you tell us whether on April 15th, 1993 you had anything to drink?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. I don't drink. I'm not an alcoholic as was stated -- as was represented by the other party, by my late wife.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you think of any reasons why your late wife and your ex-wife might have alleged that you had a drinking problem?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think that the reason for this was for her to be able to realise -- that is to get her alimony from me. For her to get money, this pension, and she had to find a reason to throw mud on me in any way, and, unfortunately, they found something which was the worst, that is they said that I was an alcoholic, that I was no good. I'm not a no-good man, I never was. Nor was anybody in my family. I was never an alcoholic. I worked. I looked after my children. I put them through school. I lived an honest life. I was good friends with all my neighbours and my acquaintances, and I can say that I always behaved in the right -- all doors were always open to me in Ljubljana, in Croatia and Serbia and Macedonia. I had friends all over the place, in all parts of the country. But, unfortunately, my late wife opted to choose this stand in order to incriminate me and to achieve her own goals. That was unfortunate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether you have any specialised training in weapons?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you were in the JNA for a period of time, were you not, Mr. Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I did my military service regularly in the army of the former JNA, the former JNA, and I was in the Noncommissioned Officers' Section. I was there for three years. And I went on the 16th of September, 1992, to the Hrvatski Karlovac area where I went to school for Reserve Officers. And there was some changes with the commander in our area, he was replaced, and he went to a -- was brought before a military court, and so my -- the managers put me in the position of Company Commander. And the 5th Military District at that time, Amnesty, reduced the term of service, so that I did not have to spend 18 months doing my military service. I returned home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us what years you were in military service in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was from 1952 to 1954. From 16th September, 1952 up to -- I don't know the exact date but it was up until 1954.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was your assignment while you were in the JNA in those months?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was the commander of the Pioneer Department, that is the student unit, afterwards, and they took me, and I performed the post of command in my unit, in the company at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And while you were in the JNA, did you obtain any kind of specialised or unique training on weapons recognition or weapon use?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. What we had was -- it was the engineer unit -- engineering unit, and we dealt with mine fields, and building bridges across rivers and that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, finally, you were asked questions about how quickly this all happened on April 16, 1993, and you testified that it did happen quickly. Can you tell us, who came into your house on April 16, 1993 and killed your family?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, the question has been asked several times, and it is the Court practice that the same thing should not be asked five times. So it's already been asked, who entered, the witness has already answered. He answered the question from the Prosecutor and he answered our questions. So I see no reason for asking the witness once again something that we started out with in his testimony. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Moskowitz, please, can you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I think, of course, this is the crucial question for the Court to consider and observe the demeanour of the witness in responding to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Also, Counsel Radovic, it is because the Defence counsel pointed to so many discrepancies between what he said in court and what he said on various occasions, so probably the -- as a follow-up to your pointing to those gaps or discrepancies or contradictions, probably it is quite appropriate for the Prosecutor, in short, to put one crucial question. So I don't think it's improper. If you don't mind, I think we should move on, because it's really the crucial question. Counsel Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I agree both with the Prosecutor and with Your Honours that it is a crucial question, but what is happening now? We indicated all the discrepancies in his statements where the crucial element was shown in a vitally different way, and now we come to the last question from the Prosecutor, which is: "Did those two do that," and he says, "Yes," and everything we did falls through, because we cannot continue to prove that what the Prosecutor had asked and the answer, whether that is true or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Please --

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: And that is why I am opposed to that question, because the question was already asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Radovic, you should please trust the Court. This is a court of professionals. We don't decide on the basis of our last impression. We, of course, weigh up all the evidence. We make a close scrutiny of what has been said in court, and we make our findings after very careful scrutiny of everything. Do trust the three professional Judges. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: All right. All right. Then I withdraw my objection to the Prosecutor's question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Moskowitz.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic. Who came into your house and killed your family?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Zoran Kupreskic came with his brother Mirjan. Zoran actually killed the family, and Mirjan set one fire, and he also started another fire, and that is how it ended.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how sure are you of that?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: One hundred per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you talked to investigators in 1993, why did you not tell them what you knew to be true?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not dare tell anyone that, for safety reasons. For the sake of my own life. I did not know what would ultimately happen and how all of that would end. I wasn't feeling safe even in the hospital in Zenica. I wondered how long we would be staying there, and I was wondering whether we would actually recover and get out of that hospital. I was wondering whether we would be bombed, shelled, whether the whole place would be set on fire, whether we would all be killed. I didn't dare tell anyone what the situation was like, because I didn't know how all of this would end. Only after the war ended in Bosnia and Herzegovina, before that, I mean, nobody could predict what would happen. That is what I wish to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ahmic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, I think that we -- you must be tired, and I'm sorry for that, we fully understand your feelings and also your sorrow for the death of your relatives. Of course, we do understand all that, but, you know, you may assist us a lot in our --

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: -- search for the truth. So if you don't mind, I would like to ask you very few questions just to clarify one or two points. First of all, where did you live in April, '93 --?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Where did you live between April '93 and the end of '94, if you can tell us?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: In the hospital, Crkvica, Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Did you spend more than one year in hospital?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you the exact date. On the 17th of April, 1993, in the afternoon, I was brought to the hospital, and I stayed there for treatment until the 1st of May, 1994. That is a bit over a year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. Now, you made three statements in 1993 about the tragic events of the 16th of April and the deaths of your relatives. Then in there you stated that you did not recognise the two persons who had killed your relatives and set fire to the house. You just told us that you did not dare tell anyone for the sake of your own life. Now my question is --

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: On the 20th of February, '94 you changed your attitude and you said to the bureau of the investigation for crimes against humanity in Vitez, that you had recognised the -- Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic. This happened, as I say, on the 20th of February, '94, while you were still in hospital. Now, my question is: What prompted you to change your mind? Why did you stop fearing for your life?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. According to the Dayton Agreement that is on the cease-fire and on ending the war, this made me feel safer, and I thought that I had no reason to fear anyone anymore. I had led an honest life, I still lead an honest life, and there is no need for me to hide from anyone that which is the truth, and I am not afraid of anyone or anything and I'm not afraid of ever stating what the truth is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Nobody doubts that you are a brave man, and in particular, that you have gone through a terrible experience. However, may I remind you that the Dayton Agreement was signed in '95, so quite a few --

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Later on. So my question is: What happened before the 20th of February, '94, which prompted you to feel safe or feel that at that stage you could tell names, I mean, tell the investigators or prosecutors, whatever, investigating judges, the names of people you thought you had recognised?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Now I can say it quite openly. Before, I did not really trust anyone. And look at us now. We're sitting here and talking, and we didn't even know each other a year ago. But probably I wouldn't have trusted you even then in those times, to tell you the truth. I didn't dare. I'm a terrified man. I was killed 70 per cent, and I went through things that nobody has gone through. I did not have the trust to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, but in this period, again, this crucial period before the 20th of February, '94, did you have an opportunity to talk to friends, relatives, about what had happened in Ahmici on the 16th of April, '93? I mean, in our countries, normally you have to talk, you need to talk to somebody about tragic events which have occurred to you. I mean, this is quite normal, to talk and to listen. So did you have an opportunity to talk?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Naturally, I did talk. I talked to all of my own people. I mean, when we were attacked and we were attacked in such a cowardly manner, it is only natural that we talked about it, but all of this was in very brief terms, our hearts were wounded, and we avoid such conversations. Until this very day, we try not to mention these things to one another. I mean, until the present day, I seek company where I can sit and talk and laugh a little bit and joke a little bit, either at my own expense or at your expense or at anybody's expense, never mind. But I try to get a few laughs in because I lost the nearest and dearest people in my whole life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Ahmic. I assume there is no objection --

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: -- to the witness being released? Again, thank you so much for coming here to give evidence in court. You have been of assistance to the court, and we are most grateful to you. Thank you. Thank you very much indeed. You may now be released.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you too, and may I thank all the gentlemen present here for all their understanding and when they were putting questions to me and when I was answering their questions, thank you all very much. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Moskowitz, I think we have time for our next witness or your next witness, who is Mr. Stevens?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stevens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: While we are waiting for Mr. Stevens, I must say that the head of the interpretation unit came to see me to say that the interpreters have a lot of difficulty in trying to interpret particularly when Defence counsel are asking questions to the witness. I am raising this issue because now Mr. Moskowitz will speak English with an Englishman, so therefore, I hope that he will also now try to stick to our rule whereby he should stop so that what the witness is going to say will be translated into Croatian, but this also applies to you, and I really make an appeal to you. Otherwise, I understand the transcript is then going to be very bad if we don't wait for the answer because the interpreters can't understand whether it is a question or an answer. All right. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Stevens. Could you please make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Examined by Mr. Moskowitz:

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please state your name and your rank for purposes of the record?

utterances.speaker: Charles Stevens
utterances.text: I am Captain Charles Stevens, known as Charlie Stevens.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Captain Stevens, I can tell by your uniform that you are in an army. Could you tell us what army you are in and give us a sense of your career and background in that army?

utterances.speaker: Charles Stevens
utterances.text: I'm currently serving in the Royal Gloucester in Wiltshire Regiment. I am a member of the British army, the infantry. I have risen through the ranks. I joined the army in September 1972. I have risen through the ranks from private soldier to captain now, my present rank.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How old are you?

utterances.speaker: Charles Stevens
utterances.text: It's my birthday today. I am 42 years old.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good. Happy Birthday.

utterances.speaker: Charles Stevens
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you give us a sense of some of the locations and countries that you've served while you were and are in the British army for the last 22 years?

utterances.speaker: Charles Stevens
utterances.text: I've served a total of six years in Northern Ireland, in Canada, Central America - Belize, Denmark, Cyprus, and that's about it. And Bosnia, obviously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. You mentioned Bosnia. When were you deployed to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: Charles Stevens
utterances.text: I arrived in Bosnia on the 13th of November, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was your rank at that time?

utterances.speaker: Charles Stevens
utterances.text: At that time, I was the Regimental Sergeant Major. I was a Warrant Officer First Class.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is a Regimental Sergeant Major?

utterances.speaker: Charles Stevens
utterances.text: A Regimental Sergeant Major is the senior soldier of the regiment. He is the highest rank soldier a non-commission soldier can rise to. There is only one in an infantry regiment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you arrived in Bosnia in November of 1992. Approximately when did you leave Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: Charles Stevens
utterances.text: I left in May 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you give us a sense of what your duties were and your assignment was while you were in Bosnia as the Regimental Sergeant Major?

utterances.speaker: Charles Stevens
utterances.text: I mentioned I arrived in November and I arrived two to three weeks after the advance party. Initially, I was concerned that we didn't have a secure base to operate from. I felt that the advance party had been distracted somewhat, had lost the fact that we need a safe place to work from, so initially, my duties were the security of the base, the structure of the base, the routine within the base, those type of duties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was the base for the regiment set up?

utterances.speaker: Charles Stevens
utterances.text: The base was set up in the school in Novi Bila.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Novi Bila is where? If you can give us a sense of what city or town it's close to?

utterances.speaker: Charles Stevens
utterances.text: It's to the north-west of Travnik, the south-west of Zenica, not over there, close to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Close to Vitez. By the way, what regiment were you attached to back then?

utterances.speaker: Charles Stevens
utterances.text: I was then with the Cheshire Regiment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you come up through the ranks with the Cheshire Regiment or through another regiment?

utterances.speaker: Charles Stevens
utterances.text: No, I came up through the ranks in the Gloucester Regiment. The Cheshire Regiment did not have a Warrant Officer Class 1 of their own. I was offered the job and I took it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it somewhat unusual for an officer to be given the regimental post of Sergeant Major of a different regiment than he originally was assigned to?

utterances.speaker: Charles Stevens
utterances.text: It hadn't been known in my particular division before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said part of your duties was to set up the camp in Novi Bila, a place near Vitez. Did you, in fact, do that, and then tell us what your duties were after that?

utterances.speaker: Charles Stevens
utterances.text: That was my first priority, to provide a safe base for the soldiers, basically. So I spent about three weeks doing that. In that time, or after that time, I became more concerned for the safety of Colonel Stewart, who -- we had never operated in an environment like this before. I perceived him to be vulnerable in many areas, so I then spent more time on his close protection, security.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned Colonel Stewart. Please tell us who he is and was.

utterances.speaker: Charles Stevens
utterances.text: Colonel Stewart was the commanding officer of the Cheshire Regiment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your function vis-à-vis Colonel Stewart while you were in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: Charles Stevens
utterances.text: My function was to provide his close security, his personal security.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How would you do that?

utterances.speaker: Charles Stevens
utterances.text: I would basically travel with him everywhere. I travelled in the rear of his armoured vehicle, and whenever he dismounted from the turret of his vehicle, I would dismount from the back and provide security for him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, while you were in Bosnia during this tour of duty, providing security for Colonel Stewart, did you have an opportunity to visit a place called Turbe?

utterances.speaker: Charles Stevens
utterances.text: I visited Turbe on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you tell us where is Turbe and what it was and what significance it had in those days?

utterances.speaker: Charles Stevens
utterances.text: Turbe was to the west of Vitez and the west of Travnik. It was the closest the Serbs had managed to get to our area. It was the closest front-line with the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe what you saw when you and Colonel Stewart travelled to Turbe?

utterances.speaker: Charles Stevens
utterances.text: We always saw an increase in the amount of forces in the area. There was always a great deal of fighting going on in that area. The main impression that I got was that it was an area that had more Muslim forces in it than any other. If I were to put a ratio to it, it was something like three-quarters Muslim army, Bosnian army, and a quarter Croatian, Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said that there was fighting going on at Turbe. Who was fighting against whom?

utterances.speaker: Charles Stevens
utterances.text: They were fighting the Serbs. The Serbs were still advancing towards Turbe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was fighting the Serbs, based upon your observation?

utterances.speaker: Charles Stevens
utterances.text: Based upon my observation, in the main, the Bosnian Muslim army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see much of a presence of the HVO or the Croatian army in Turbe?

utterances.speaker: Charles Stevens
utterances.text: I didn't see a presence in terms of large numbers of troops.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see a presence of the HVO in other areas in and around your operational area?

utterances.speaker: Charles Stevens
utterances.text: There was always a great number of troops in Vitez area generally and other areas that were away from the front-line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of troops did you see in the Vitez area?

utterances.speaker: Charles Stevens
utterances.text: All sorts. I wasn't able to determine which units they were from. Predominantly Croatian forces, HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were in the operational area for the six months or so from November to May, do you recall an incident involving the shelling of Zenica?

utterances.speaker: Charles Stevens
utterances.text: Yes, I do. That was towards the end of our tour. I travelled an awful lot with Colonel Stewart. Basically everywhere there was travel or a need, I went. In the latter part of the tour, I did start to lose some degree of, you know -- not orientation but track of time, so it was towards the end of the tour. I would say after, after the Easter break, Easter holidays, when things seemed to sort of get out of hand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you recall about the shelling of Zenica, which you recall as happening towards the end of your tour?

utterances.speaker: Charles Stevens
utterances.text: I recall that on a Sunday morning, an artillery piece close to our base opened fire. This artillery piece had been silent for some time. Through our operations room, I heard that Zenica had been shelled. At this stage, at this time, there was supposed to be a cease-fire in operation. I was extremely angry about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why were you angry about it?

utterances.speaker: Charles Stevens
utterances.text: I was angry because this was a cease-fire that we thought, BRITBAT thought, might hold. I was angry because it was a Sunday, a religious day, and I had become angry at things that I had seen throughout the whole six months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what did you do, if anything, after you had heard that Zenica had been shelled?

utterances.speaker: Charles Stevens
utterances.text: Unusually, I called for another warrant officer and an interpreter and left the base to find the location of the gun.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have an idea of where this gun might be located and who the gun belonged to?

utterances.speaker: Charles Stevens
utterances.text: The gun belonged to the HVO, and it was between 150 -- a kilometre and a half and two kilometres from our base.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you then do?

utterances.speaker: Charles Stevens
utterances.text: I took the Sergeant Major and an interpreter with me to try to get close to the gun and find out if there was an officer there, and for him to point out on a map to me the target that he was firing at.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you find an officer in the vicinity of the gun?

utterances.speaker: Charles Stevens
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I found three or four men, all who denied being in charge, and I asked them to get me an officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say three or four men, were these soldiers?

utterances.speaker: Charles Stevens
utterances.text: They were soldiers dressed in HVO uniform operating some sort of checkpoint before the gun.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they allow you to go through the checkpoint to examine the weapon?

utterances.speaker: Charles Stevens
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did they tell you?

utterances.speaker: Charles Stevens
utterances.text: They told me that I couldn't -- I couldn't see the gun, I was not to move from the position, at which point I demanded that an officer come up to explain what was happening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then what happened?

utterances.speaker: Charles Stevens
utterances.text: Some 15 to 20 minutes later, an officer arrived in a car. He wouldn't speak to me there, but he would speak to me in a small cafe-type place further away. So I got in the car with him with the other two people and drove off to this cafe to sit outside it and get the maps out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he tell you, this soldier?

utterances.speaker: Charles Stevens
utterances.text: He told me through the interpreter that he was a professional artillery officer, an ex-JNA, and that he was firing at targets in the Brcko or Brdo feature. There was a mountain there on the map. I then radioed through to the ops room to try to get that confirmed, and I was told there was no -- there was no firing in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you didn't believe him?

utterances.speaker: Charles Stevens
utterances.text: No, I didn't, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did this conversation end and what did you do?

utterances.speaker: Charles Stevens
utterances.text: The conversation -- I did -- I thought I had some sort of rapport with him. He had a bad case of eczema. I had access to medical stores. So I basically talked about his skin disorder, got him some -- at a later point sent him some cream in the hope that I could sort of -- that he would tell me what targets he was firing at.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he ever tell you what target he was firing at?

utterances.speaker: Charles Stevens
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were in this operational area during this time period, do you recall an incident that occurred in the town of Vitez involving a bomb?

utterances.speaker: Charles Stevens
utterances.text: I recall an incident, again round about the middle of April onwards, that a petrol tanker had been exploded in the Muslim part, the western part of Vitez, that this tanker had been placed near what was thought to be a munitions dump. I was told -- I arrived on the scene the day after this explosion, and I was told by local militia-type forces that two Muslims had been strapped into the cab of the tanker, chained in there, and the HVO fired RPG-7 rounds into the back to cause the explosion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see the effects of the explosion?

utterances.speaker: Charles Stevens
utterances.text: I did, yes. Massive destruction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This would be in what part of Vitez; do you know?

utterances.speaker: Charles Stevens
utterances.text: This would be the western part, in the Muslim -- generally the Muslim side of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: At this time, I would ask the usher to show the witness the following exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Ms. Slokovic-Glumac?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecutor is actually trying to present proof in connection with events that took place after the 16th; that is to say, the 18th of April and the shelling of Zenica at the end of April. So I think that these are not circumstances that are relevant to our indictment because our indictment refers to the 16th of April, 1993. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Moskowitz?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: We believe these incidents are relevant on several grounds: First, there have been statements from witnesses taken shortly after the incident in Ahmici, and the witnesses are explaining why there are some discrepancies in the statements and some of those explanations involve the ongoing war and the shelling of Zenica and the bombing in and around the Vitez area that caused them great fear and concern, and so this is being offered to demonstrate that, in fact, this was going on at that time after the Ahmici massacre. The incident in Ahmici is part of our indictment, it's certainly the main part of our indictment, but the indictment also talks about ethnic cleansing throughout the Lasva Valley, and this truck bomb in Vitez and the shelling in Zenica constitute evidence of the greater ethnic cleansing operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. Yes, you may proceed. This is quite a convincing explanation. However, I would not -- since this is not the focus of our case, I wonder whether you could move on quickly to other questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: We will move quickly through this, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 160.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Captain Stevens, could you look at that photograph that's been placed next to you and see if you can describe what that depicts?

utterances.speaker: Charles Stevens
utterances.text: I can confirm that that's a picture of the site of that tanker explosion. It's pretty similar on all sides, so within a radius of the road, that was the scene.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this a fair and accurate portrayal of the scene in the Muslim part of Zenica following the truck bomb as you remember it?

utterances.speaker: Charles Stevens
utterances.text: Completely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could you also tell us whether or not you personally saw any evidence of ethnic cleansing in and around the British camp in Novi Bila near Vitez while you were in the operational area?

utterances.speaker: Charles Stevens
utterances.text: Again, towards the end of the tour -- as I mentioned earlier, I was quite angry with the way that the situation was developing around the base. I regarded it as the only piece of area we could protect. At this time, there seemed to be a build-up of refugees on both sides of the camp, Muslims on one side and Croatians on the other side. Close to the end of the tour, from the Croatian side of Novi Bila, they made an effort to cleanse those people that lived by the side of the camp. On one occasion, they attempted to -- they started an attack that would run alongside the base clearing people out of their houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said "they" made an effort. Who do you mean by "they"?

utterances.speaker: Charles Stevens
utterances.text: The local HVO forces in Novi Bila.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did they conduct that effort, to clean out the Muslims that were located near your camp?

utterances.speaker: Charles Stevens
utterances.text: I came across a section of eight to ten of them. It was brought to my attention by sentries close to the entrance to the camp. The Muslims in that area adopted a defensive-type position in a trench with the one rifle that they had in that area. I went out between -- I stepped into the road between both sides with my hand up trying to stop them opening fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened?

utterances.speaker: Charles Stevens
utterances.text: I sent the HVO back to their previous position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you do anything more to try to stop this kind of ethnic cleansing from coming again or repeating?

utterances.speaker: Charles Stevens
utterances.text: Yeah. The situation at that time was -- the fighting was ferocious just about everywhere in the valleys around the base, and all the more senior officers were involved in that. I took it upon myself to produce a document that I could take to both sides to try and secure a thousand-metre exclusion zone around the camp, a demilitarised zone, if you like, and I took that document to the local HVO group.
